cards.b: Product, price, place and promotion, combined consistently to satisfy the target market.
Brand image: personality given to a product that distinguishes it. Brand loyalty: consumers keep buying the same brand.
Low sales and usually a loss due to high development and promotion costs. Informative advertising; skimming or penetration pricing.
Used at maturity/saturation: new markets, new uses, redesign, new packaging, target another segment, more advertising or promotion.
Unit cost plus a percentage mark-up. Cost €8 + 25% = €10. Ignores competitors' prices and demand.
Low price on launch to gain market share, then raised. Suits a mass market and new entrants.
High price at launch for a new or unique product, lowered later. Suits innovative products and strong brands.
Competitive: price near competitors'. Promotional: low price for a short time (e.g. buy one get one free) to clear stock.
Quantity demanded changes by a bigger percentage than price. A price cut raises revenue.
Quantity demanded changes by a smaller percentage than price (it still changes). A price rise raises revenue.
Producer sells straight to the consumer (e.g. online). Producer keeps full profit and control.
Producer → wholesaler → retailer → consumer. Suits many small, spread-out shops.
Informative: gives facts (e.g. new product). Persuasive: tries to convince customers to buy and builds brand image.
Incentives to encourage short-term sales: discounts, coupons, free samples, buy one get one free, competitions.

gaps.s: The four Ps are product, price, place and ___ .
A product that makes a loss in the early stage is usually in the ___ stage of its life cycle.
A unit cost of €8 with a 25% mark-up gives a cost-plus price of € ___ .
Setting a low price to enter a new market is ___ pricing.
A very high launch price for a new, innovative product is price ___ .
If demand is price-___ , a price rise increases revenue.
The route a product takes from producer to customer is the channel of ___ .
Money planned to be spent on marketing over a period is the marketing ___ .

short.q: Explain one reason why a business may want to develop a new product. [2]
short.model: New products attract new customers, raising sales and market share. They also spread risk across a wider product range.

short.q: Explain one extension strategy a business could use for a product in the saturation stage. [3]
short.model: The business could redesign the product or find a new market such as exporting. This attracts new customers and delays decline in sales.

short.q: Calculate the selling price using cost-plus pricing with a unit cost of €12 and a 40% mark-up. [2]
A product has price-inelastic demand. Explain what this means for a business that raises its price. [3]
short.model: Quantity demanded falls by a smaller percentage than the price rise, so revenue increases.
points: % fall in quantity smaller than % rise in price

short.q: Explain two advantages to a business of selling online (e-commerce). [4]
short.model: It can reach a global market and open 24 hours. It saves the cost of a shop and collects customer data.
